section.title: A Good Name
section.sectionRationale: These sixteen verses close the first Solomonic collection, 10:1 to 22:16, before the book turns to the Sayings of the Wise. The chapter opens by ranking a good name above riches, moves through the shared humanity of rich and poor under their Maker, the training of a child, and closes with warnings against oppressing the poor for gain.
section.thesis: A good name and the fear of the LORD outweigh riches, since rich and poor alike are made by the same LORD, and wisdom trains children early, gives generously, and refuses to build a future on oppression of the poor.
section.frameNote: Four clusters: a good name above riches, and the common Maker of rich and poor; prudence, humility, and the discipline of a child; generosity, hospitality, and driving out the mocker; the deep pit of the adulteress, and warnings against oppressing the poor.

units.label: A good name above riches
units.note: the common Maker of rich and poor

verses.text: A good name is more desirable than great riches; favor is better than silver and gold.
The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is Maker of them all.
The prudent see danger and take cover, but the simple keep going and suffer the consequences.
The rewards of humility and the {{yirah|fear}} of the LORD are wealth and honor and life.

units.label: Prudence and the training of a child
units.note: guard your soul, train up a child

verses.text: Thorns and snares lie on the path of the perverse; he who guards his soul stays far from them.
Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.
The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender.
He who sows injustice will reap disaster, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed.

units.label: Generosity and driving out the mocker
units.note: a generous man will be blessed

verses.text: A generous man will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.
Drive out the mocker, and conflict will depart; even quarreling and insults will cease.
He who loves a pure heart and gracious lips will have the king for a friend.
The LORD's eyes keep watch over knowledge, but He frustrates the words of the faithless.

units.label: Warnings against oppressing the poor
units.note: the deep pit and the rod of discipline

verses.text: The slacker says, "There is a lion outside! I will be slain in the streets!"
The mouth of an adulteress is a deep pit; he who is under the wrath of the LORD will fall into it.
Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.
Oppressing the poor to enrich oneself or giving gifts to the rich will surely lead to poverty.

yirah.gloss: Fear, reverent awe of God. Verse 4 pairs this fear with humility as the twin roots that yield wealth, honor, and life, the same fear named in Proverbs 1:7 as the beginning of knowledge, showing that true reward flows from reverence, not from grasping or self-promotion.

basic.context: This short section closes the long first collection of Solomon's proverbs. It opens with a striking priority, a good name and God's favor outrank silver and gold, and grounds human equality in the fact that the LORD made both rich and poor. From there it moves through the training of children and closes with sharp warnings against oppressing the poor for personal gain.
basic.hermeneutics: These are wisdom generalizations describing how life under God tends to reward humility, generosity, and careful child training, and tends to punish injustice and oppression. Verse 6, 'train up a child... he will not depart,' is widely misread as an ironclad promise; Proverbs' own genre and the broader witness of Scripture, including children who reject good training, show it describes a normal pattern of formation rather than an unconditional guarantee.
basic.originalLanguages: Yirah, the fear of the LORD, verse 4, is paired with humility as the root of true reward, wealth, honor, and life, echoing the refrain that runs through the whole book. The chapter's insistence that the LORD is Maker of both rich and poor, verse 2, uses the same verb for God's creative work found in Genesis, grounding human dignity in shared origin rather than social status.
basic.typology: The good name prized above riches, verse 1, anticipates the name of Jesus, above every name, in which alone true and lasting favor is found, Philippians 2:9-11. The common Maker of rich and poor, verse 2, foreshadows the gospel's leveling of all people before the cross, where neither wealth nor poverty grants standing before God, only grace received by faith.
basic.christ: Verse 1's good name, worth more than silver and gold, finds its ultimate referent in the name of Jesus, given the name above every name, at which every knee will bow, Philippians 2:9 to 11, the name in which alone true and lasting favor is secured. And verse 2's declaration that the LORD is Maker of both rich and poor anticipates the gospel truth that at the foot of the cross all human distinctions of wealth and status collapse before the one Savior who died for both, Galatians 3:28.
basic.god: God is the Maker of rich and poor alike, verse 2, refusing any human hierarchy of worth based on wealth, and He rewards humility and reverent fear with true wealth, honor, and life, verse 4. He watches over knowledge and frustrates the schemes of the faithless, verse 12, and His anger burns against those who oppress the poor to enrich themselves, verse 16.
basic.crossReferences: Philippians 2:9-11 exalts the name above every name, the ultimate good name of verse 1. Galatians 3:28 echoes the shared humanity of rich and poor before God, verse 2. Ephesians 6:4 develops verse 6's training of children with a father's tender restraint. James 2:1-9 echoes verse 16's warning against favoring the rich and oppressing the poor.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 22:1 to 16 prizes a good name, humble fear of the LORD, and generous care for the poor over wealth gained by injustice. The whole story of Scripture answers with the name of Jesus, exalted above every name, in whom rich and poor alike, sharing one Maker, find the true and lasting favor no money can buy.

context.literary:
These sixteen verses are the last stretch of a collection that opened at 10:1 with the title 'The proverbs of Solomon'. At 22:17 the voice changes to a longer address, 'Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise', and the sayings run in groups of a few lines. So the passage is a closing section, and it reads like one: it gathers the collection's main themes in small, and it begins and ends on the same subject, money.

Verses 1 and 2 are a pair. Verse 1 ranks a good name above riches, and verse 2 grounds the ranking in a fact about the Maker of the rich and poor. Verse 16 returns to the subject from the opposite side, with the rich who oppress the poor and the generous who give to the rich both ending in lack. The frame therefore runs from the value of a name to the cost of exploitation.

Inside the frame are small clusters. Verses 3 to 5 are about foresight: the prudent take cover, the humble fear the LORD, and the perverse walk among thorns. Verses 6 to 8 move to the household, the child trained, the borrower enslaved and the sower of injustice. Verses 9 to 12 are about speech and the court, ending with the LORD's eyes keeping watch. Verses 13 to 16 are a set of warnings: the slacker's excuse, the pit of the adulteress, the child's folly and the oppressor's loss.

Several lines are repeats or near repeats of other proverbs: verse 3 is 27:12 almost exactly, verse 13 is a form of 26:13, and verse 11 echoes the king's favour for the pure of 16:13. The sages reused what they trusted.
context.historical:
A name in ancient Israel was more than a label. It carried a family's honour, its standing in the gate, and its claim on the land. The preacher's line in Ecclesiastes 7:1, 'A good name is better than fine perfume', and Proverbs 22:1 share a conviction that reputation outlasts what a person owns. A good name here is 'favour', chen, in the eyes of others, so it means being trusted in a community where trust was currency.

Debt was a real threat. Verse 7, 'the borrower is slave to the lender', describes a world in which a failed harvest could send a family into borrowing and a borrower into servitude. The widow of a prophet in 2 Kings 4:1 found her creditor coming to take her two sons as slaves, and Nehemiah 5:1 to 5 shows farmers mortgaging their fields and selling their children to pay the king's tax and buy grain. The law had provisions for release and against interest, Exodus 22:25, but the sages knew the law was often broken.

Teaching a child was a household task. Moses had told Israel to teach God's words diligently to their children, 'when you sit at home and when you walk along the road', Deuteronomy 6:7. The training of verse 6 belonged in the family, and the discipline of verse 15 was the ordinary tool of that training in the ancient world, as in many cultures since.

Verse 11 speaks of the king. In the court a person of pure heart and gracious speech would be a trusted adviser. The collection's reference to the king here and in many chapters shows that it was in part a handbook for the young who would serve at court.

Verse 14's adulteress belongs to the book's long warning, 2:16 to 19, 5:3 to 6, 7:6 to 27, and the word used in Hebrew for her in the opening chapters, 'foreign' or 'strange', may suggest someone outside the covenant community.
context.canonical:
The good name of verse 1 travels through the whole canon. Ecclesiastes 7:1 turns it, and the Gospel of Luke says of the boy Jesus that He 'grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man', Luke 2:52, the same pair of favours the proverb praises. Philippians 2:9 to 11 gives Jesus 'the name above all names'.

Verse 2 is the Old Testament's recurring ground for treating the poor justly. Job asks of his servants, 'Did not He who made me in the womb also make them?', Job 31:15, Proverbs 14:31 says that whoever oppresses the poor taunts his Maker, and 29:13 says the poor man and the oppressor have this in common, that the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. Paul preaches to Athens that God 'made every nation of men' from one, Acts 17:26, and writes to the churches that in Christ there is neither slave nor free, Galatians 3:28. James 2:1 to 9 applies the principle to the seating arrangements of a meeting.

Verse 6 sits with Deuteronomy 6:6 to 7 and Ephesians 6:4, and Paul reminds Timothy that from infancy he had known the Holy Scriptures, 2 Timothy 3:15. Verse 8 and verse 16 anticipate Paul's 'Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return', Galatians 6:7. The BSB footnote on verse 8 observes that the Septuagint adds a line, 'God blesses a cheerful and generous man', and directs the reader to 2 Corinthians 9:7, where Paul writes that 'God loves a cheerful giver'. Whether or not Paul had that Greek line in mind, the teaching is the same as verse 9: generosity is blessed.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sage means to close the long collection with a clear order of values. A good name comes before money, the fear of the LORD comes before status, and the poor man is the neighbour of the rich, made by the same hand. The hearer is not being told that money is bad, but that money cannot be the measure of anything that matters. The first four verses give the standard, and the last twelve show what living by it looks like in a household and in a town.

He also means to teach prudence. Verse 3 is blunt: the prudent see danger and take cover, and the simple walk on and pay for it. This is not cowardice but the ability to read the road. Verse 5 says the same of moral danger, thorns and snares for the perverse, and the person who guards his soul stays far off. In this sense wisdom is as much about distance as about courage.

Finally, he wants a hearer to take responsibility for the next generation. Verse 6 and verse 15 are addressed to parents, and verse 9 and verse 16 to anyone who has more than he needs. The close of the collection is a call to give and to form others, and the warning about oppressing the poor is the sharpest edge of it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This section blends commands and observations, and it is easy to misread them. Verse 6 is stated as a command to train a child, and the second half is a promise of a general kind. It is a statement of how formation tends to work, not a legal guarantee of the adult's choices. Parents who did their best and have grieving hearts should not be told that the proverb has failed, and parents who did little should not be told that the outcome was never their concern.

Verse 7 is a plain description, 'the rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender'. It does not say that this is how things ought to be. Taken with verse 16 and with the law's restraints on lending, it warns the borrower of the real cost of debt and the lender of the power he holds. It is a caution to read the economy honestly.

Verse 15 is the one that causes most discomfort. It says foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child and the rod of discipline drives it far from him. The rod language belongs to its world, and the rest of Scripture lays down the spirit in which discipline is to be given, Ephesians 6:4 and Colossians 3:21. What carries over is the conviction that children need patient, consistent correction, and that love includes it.

Verse 13 is a comic portrait. The slacker's lion is an excuse, not a command. We should read it as a description of how an idle person talks himself out of work, and not as a rule about danger.

debates.question: What does 'in the way he should go' mean in verse 6?

views.label: The right way, the path of wisdom and godliness
views.case: The BSB takes 'way' as the proper path, as 'way' means throughout Proverbs, for example 4:11 and 4:26. Parents train the child in the path of wisdom, and the promise is that early formation sticks.

views.label: The way suited to the child's own bent
views.case: The Hebrew says literally something close to 'according to his way', and some take this to mean a path matched to the child's own temperament and gifts. Training is then wise attention to the individual, not one pattern for all children.

views.label: His own way, so that training works with his nature and not against it
views.case: Read this way the proverb warns that what a child is allowed to become in youth is what he will be in age, so that the formation of habit is the point more than the choice of path.

debates.bearing: The first reading best fits the book, where 'way' is usually a moral path. The second reminds parents that wisdom is not a single formula. Neither makes the verse a guarantee: Proverbs elsewhere shows sons who reject good teaching, such as 10:1 and 15:20, and 1 Samuel 8:3 records a godly man's sons who went astray.

debates.question: Are the two halves of verse 16 one sin or two?

views.label: Two ways of reaching the same ruin
views.case: The BSB reads two kinds of act that both end in loss: oppressing the poor to get rich, and giving gifts to the rich to win favour. Both are attempts to rise by wrong means.

views.label: One act: oppressing the poor and then bribing the rich to protect the gain
views.case: A person who exploits the poor then buys the protection of the powerful. Both halves describe one crooked strategy that fails.

views.label: The Hebrew is too compressed to be sure
views.case: The line has no connecting words in the original, and translators fill the gap differently. The safe conclusion is the one every reading shares: wrongful gain ends in lack.

debates.bearing: The practical teaching is the same either way: the poor are not a source to be mined, and flattering the wealthy is no substitute for honest work. It sits at the end of the passage as a warning aimed at the ambitious.

study.originalLanguages:
In verse 2 the BSB says the rich and the poor 'have this in common', but the verb in Hebrew is nifgashu, 'they meet'. The proverb pictures rich and poor meeting, as they must in any town, and says what they meet over: the LORD is the Maker of them all. The word for 'Maker' is the participle of asah, 'to make or do', the ordinary verb for creating, and the verb is used in the same way in Proverbs 14:31 and 17:5. That the poor man has a Maker at all is the ground of his dignity.

Verse 4 begins with eqev, which the BSB renders 'the rewards'. The same word means 'consequence' or 'as a result', and it shares its letters with the word for heel. In Genesis 22:18 it carries the sense 'because you obeyed'. So the verse says what follows on the heels of humility and the fear of the LORD: wealth, honour and life. It is the book's conviction that a godly character has outcomes.

Verse 6 has the verb chanokh, 'train', from a root that elsewhere means to dedicate, as when a new house or an altar is dedicated, Deuteronomy 20:5 and 1 Kings 8:63. The idea is of setting a thing apart for its purpose and giving it its first use. The child is called a na'ar, a word that stretches from an infant, Exodus 2:6, to a young man. And 'in the way he should go' translates 'al pi darko, literally 'according to the mouth of his way', which is why readers differ on whether 'his way' is the proper path or his own bent.

Verse 9 describes the generous man as tov ayin, 'good of eye', which the BSB footnote gives as 'He whose eye is good'. The opposite, ra ayin, 'evil of eye', is the grudging, as in 23:6 and 28:22. The eye here is the organ of generosity or envy. The verse adds that he 'gives of his bread', and the verb is simple: nathan. The Septuagint extends verse 8 with a line about God blessing a cheerful and generous man, as the BSB footnote notes, and the footnote points to 2 Corinthians 9:7.

Verse 10 tells the community to 'drive out' the mocker, garesh, the verb used when Sarah demanded that Hagar and her son be sent away, Genesis 21:10. It is strong, a verb of expulsion, and it makes the passage's point: a scoffer can contaminate a community until he is removed.

In verse 14 the adulteress is literally a 'strange' or 'foreign' woman, zarah, the word used in the opening chapters of the book, 2:16. Her mouth is a deep pit, shuchah amuqah, and the wrath of the LORD, za'um, is the force that lets a man fall into it.

typology.type: The good name above great riches, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: A name valued above silver and gold is the very pattern of how Scripture speaks of the Son. 'God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names', Philippians 2:9, and Peter says that salvation is in no other name, Acts 4:12. The escalation is that Jesus' name is not only esteemed but saving. A good name in Proverbs gives favour among people; His gives access to God. The type is surpassed because even the best reputation could not undo a person's sin, while His name can be called on by anyone, Romans 10:13.

typology.type: The Maker of rich and poor, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The shared Maker is not only a doctrine of creation but a promise of a shared Redeemer. In Christ, 'there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female', Galatians 3:28, and James tells the church not to hold out faith in the glorious Lord Jesus while showing favouritism, James 2:1. The rich and poor who met in the market meet in the same community at the table of the Lord. The correspondence falls short of the whole gospel at one point: creation gives equal dignity, but only Christ gives equal standing before God as a gift.

typology.type: The generous man who shares his bread, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The man of good eye who shares with the poor anticipates the One who fed a crowd with a boy's few loaves and who taught that it is more blessed to give than to receive, Acts 20:35. The escalation is in the scale of generosity: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor', 2 Corinthians 8:9. The type falls short in that the proverb's giver shares from what he has, while Christ gives Himself, and the bread He shares is His own flesh, John 6:51.

study.christ:
This passage is about a good name, a shared Maker, generosity and the training of children, and each leads toward Christ in a different way. As elsewhere in Proverbs, none of them is a direct prediction, so the links have to be drawn through texts that the New Testament itself provides.

The good name comes first. Verse 1 says favour is better than silver and gold. Luke records of the boy Jesus that He 'grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man', Luke 2:52, which is exactly the double favour the sage commends. Jesus is the one person whose name was never in need of repair. Yet He gave it up. Isaiah says He was despised and rejected, and on the cross He bore a name that was not His own, as a criminal. Philippians 2:6 to 11 then tells the pattern: the one who emptied Himself is given the name above all names. The path to the good name in Proverbs, humility and the fear of the LORD, verse 4, is the exact path of Christ, who 'humbled Himself' and was exalted.

Verse 2 leads to Christ in a different way, through the Maker. John says all things were made through the Word, John 1:3, and Colossians 1:16 says all things were created through Him and for Him. The Maker of rich and poor, in the New Testament, is the Son. Since the poor are made by Him, Matthew 25:40, His identification with them is not charity from a distance but the Maker visiting what He made.

Verse 9 and verse 16 lead to His giving. He gave bread to the hungry, and He gave Himself, and for Paul the supreme example of generosity is Christ who became poor so we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The person with a good eye in the proverb is a small portrait of the Giver.

Verse 6 and verse 15 on the training of children bring Christ in as the one who was Himself taught and who now disciplines and teaches His people. Hebrews 12:7 reads discipline as the treatment of sons. Be careful not to press every line: the adulteress's pit and the lion in the street are matters of practical wisdom, not hidden gospel.
study.god:
The passage shows God as Maker first. Verse 2 says that the LORD is the Maker of rich and poor, and everything in the passage about wealth, status and power is judged by that fact. A God who made both will not see the one as more important than the other. He is therefore also the Defender of the one who has fewer defenders. Verse 16 is a warning that the LORD takes the poor man's side, and 22:22 to 23, just after the passage, says in so many words that He will take up the case of the afflicted.

He is also the One who watches. Verse 12 says His eyes keep watch over knowledge, and He frustrates the words of the faithless. The sentence is about truth: God guards what is known and true and overturns what is false. In a section full of schemes and excuses, this is a promise that lies do not last.

He rewards, but not as a vending machine. Verse 4 says that humility and the fear of the LORD bring wealth, honour and life, and verse 9 says that the generous man is blessed. The language is of a God who builds consequences into the world He made and also acts in it. The sower of injustice reaps disaster, verse 8, and the rod of his fury is destroyed. God is both the architect of the moral order and a participant in it.

And He is angry at what destroys people. The 'wrath of the LORD', verse 14, is the force beneath the pit, and the oppression of the poor in verse 16 is not a neutral economic fact but an offence against the Maker. The God of the passage is neither sentimental nor harsh: He opposes what harms those He made.

For worship, this means that how we treat the poor, the debtor and the child is a matter of worship, not only ethics. It also means a gentle confidence for parents and for the poor: the LORD is the one who watches over what the powerful overlook. To fear Him, verse 4, is to be freed from the fear of people who think they own others.

crossReferences.note: A good name is better than fine perfume. It repeats the ranking of verse 1 in the voice of the Preacher, who adds the sober thought that the day of death is better than the day of birth, because a name can only be judged at the end.

Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honours Him. It builds on verse 2 by making the fact of a shared Maker a reason for conduct: the poor man is made by the One who answers for him.

Job says that if he had rejected the case of his servants, he would not know what to answer when God rises to judge, for the same One who made him made them. It is a lived example of verse 2, an employer who treats his servants as his equals before the Maker.

Paul tells the Athenians that God made every nation from one man. It widens verse 2 from rich and poor to all peoples, and it shows that the creation of everyone by one Maker is a basis for the apostolic message.
There is neither slave nor free, for all are one in Christ Jesus. It does for the church what verse 2 does for creation, and it keeps the social differences from deciding who belongs.

God's words are to be on the heart and taught diligently to children at home and on the road. It is the pattern of the training in verse 6, showing that early formation in Israel meant daily conversation, not only instruction.
Fathers are not to provoke their children to wrath but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. It keeps verse 15 within bounds by naming the aim and spirit of correction.

Samuel's sons did not walk in his ways but took bribes and perverted justice. It is the standing example of a godly man whose children went wrong, and it prevents verse 6 from being read as a guarantee.

Each should give as he has decided in his heart, not from regret or compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. The BSB footnote on Proverbs 22:8 points here, because the Greek text of that verse adds a similar line about a cheerful and generous man. Paul's teaching matches verse 9's generous man.

James warns against giving the seat of honour to the man in fine clothes and telling the poor man to stand. It is verse 2 and verse 16 turned into a scene from a church meeting, where partiality is called a failure of faith.
Do not rob a poor man because he is poor, for the LORD will take up their case. It follows the passage immediately and spells out the threat in verse 16: the oppressed have a Defender who acts.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 22:1 to 16 begins where Genesis begins, with a Maker. Verse 2 tells us that rich and poor have one source, and the first chapters of the Bible tell the same story of creation: every person is made in God's image, Genesis 1:27, and there are no grades of humanity. The fall broke that unity and set up the world the passage describes, with debt, exploitation and the strong ruling the weak. Cain's question, 'Am I my brother's keeper?', is the question of verses 9 and 16 in its first form.

The covenant law answers by forming a people who are meant to remember the poor. The Sabbath year, the ban on interest, the gleaning laws and the cry of the oppressed that God hears all belong to Israel's story. The sages take what the law commands and teach it as wisdom: a good name is built by justice, and the generous are blessed. When Israel failed, the prophets, in Amos, Isaiah and Micah, accused it of the very sins verse 16 names.

The story then moves to Christ. The Maker of rich and poor became a poor man, a carpenter's son born among animals, who had nowhere to lay His head. He took a name that was despised, and God made it the name above all names. He taught that giving is blessed, and He gave everything. The church formed by Him is told to treat rich and poor alike, and the early believers shared what they had, Acts 2:44 to 45. The training of children passes to the household of faith, where parents bring up the young in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

The new creation is the end of verse 7's world. No one is a slave to a lender because every debt is cancelled, and there is no more oppression of the poor. Revelation 7:16 promises that they will hunger no more, and 21:4 that every tear is wiped away. The good name that people wanted all their lives is given: the redeemed bear the Lamb's name on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4, and the Maker of them all is with them.

quiz.q: What does verse 1 say is more desirable than great riches?

options.text: A good name, and favor better than silver and gold.
options.note: Reputation and God's favor are ranked above material wealth.

options.text: A large inheritance.
options.note: The verse ranks a good name above riches, not equates them.

options.text: Physical strength.
options.note: Strength is not the topic of this verse.

options.text: A good name, valued about equally with riches.
options.note: The verse ranks a good name clearly above riches, not merely equal to them.

quiz.q: What do rich and poor have in common according to verse 2?

options.text: The LORD is Maker of them all.
options.note: Shared origin in God grounds equal human dignity regardless of wealth.

options.text: They share equal amounts of wealth over time.
options.note: The verse addresses shared origin, not economic equality.

options.text: They are equally prone to laziness.
options.note: This is not the point the verse is making.

options.text: They will eventually become equally wealthy.
options.note: The verse's point is about common creation by God, not eventual economic leveling.

quiz.q: What does verse 6 counsel about training a child?

options.text: Train up a child in the way he should go, so that when he is old he will not depart from it.
options.note: Early, consistent moral formation is commended as normally shaping a person's whole life.

options.text: Children should be left to choose their own way without guidance.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the verse commends.

options.text: Only formal education matters for a child's future.
options.note: The verse speaks broadly of moral and spiritual training, not formal education specifically.

options.text: Training guarantees a child's future choices with no exceptions.
options.note: Read alongside the rest of Scripture, this states a general pattern rather than an unconditional, exception-free guarantee.

quiz.q: What does verse 9 say about the generous man?

options.text: He will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.
options.note: Generosity toward the poor is directly tied to blessing.

options.text: He will lose everything by giving too much away.
options.note: This is the opposite of the promise in the verse.

options.text: He should give only to those who can repay him.
options.note: The verse commends sharing bread with the poor, who by definition cannot repay.

options.text: He is blessed only if his generosity is publicly recognized.
options.note: The verse attaches no condition of public recognition to the blessing described.

quiz.q: What warning does verse 16 give about wealth?

options.text: Oppressing the poor to enrich oneself, or giving gifts to the rich, will surely lead to poverty.
options.note: Unjust methods of gaining wealth ultimately backfire.

options.text: All forms of wealth accumulation lead to poverty.
options.note: The verse specifically targets unjust methods, not wealth in general.

options.text: Giving gifts to the rich always increases one's own wealth.
options.note: The verse says the opposite, that this leads to poverty.

options.text: Oppressing the poor is only wrong if it becomes publicly known.
options.note: The verse states the consequence as a moral certainty, not contingent on public discovery.

questions: Verse 1 ranks a good name above riches. Where are you currently tempted to trade your integrity for financial gain or advancement?
Verse 2 says the LORD is Maker of both rich and poor. How does this truth challenge the way you view or treat people of different economic status?
Verse 6 speaks of training a child in the way he should go. If you are raising or influencing children, what is one habit of training you need to be more consistent about?
Verse 9 blesses the one who shares bread with the poor. What would practical, costly generosity look like for you this month?

Verse 16 warns against enriching yourself by oppressing the poor. Are there any of your financial habits, spending, business, or investment choices, that indirectly depend on someone else's exploitation?

translationNotes.note: 'A good name' translates shem tov, literally 'a good name,' a phrase carrying the weight of reputation, family honor, and covenant identity, not mere popularity.
'In the way he should go' can also be rendered 'according to his way,' possibly meaning suited to the child's own bent or stage, a nuance debated among Hebrew scholars.
'The mouth of an adulteress is a deep pit' anticipates the extended warning against the adulteress developed further in the discourses of chapters 2, 5, and 7.
